title: Supreme Court Will Finally Decide Whether the State Can Run Hindu Temples
excerpt: After 13 years of delays, a constitutional challenge to government control over temples in four southern states is back before the highest bench.
body:
For thirteen years, a fundamental question about religious freedom in India has been stuck in legal limbo: can state governments appoint officers, audit accounts, and control the surplus funds of Hindu temples? On Monday, the Supreme Court decided it was finally time to answer it.

A bench of Justices BV Nagarathna and Satish Chandra Sharma revived a batch of petitions challenging laws that give state governments sweeping administrative power over Hindu temples and religious endowments in Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, and Puducherry. The case — *Swami Dayananda Saraswathi vs State of Tamil Nadu* — was originally filed in 2012 and has been through multiple rounds of procedural delays, including an April 2025 order that sent the petitioners back to their respective High Courts.

That order has now been recalled. The Supreme Court will hear the challenge on its merits.

## What the Laws Actually Do

The statutes under challenge — the Tamil Nadu Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act (1959), the Andhra Pradesh Charitable and Hindu Religious Institutions and Endowments Act (1987), and their Telangana and Puducherry equivalents — give state-appointed Commissioners and Executive Officers significant control over temple administration.

These officials can audit temple finances, appoint trustees, manage surplus revenue, approve or block the alienation of temple property, and in some cases direct how temple funds are spent. The laws apply to Hindu institutions specifically — mosques, churches, and gurudwaras are not covered by equivalent legislation, a disparity that the petitioners argue violates Article 14 of the Constitution, which guarantees equality before the law.

The petitioners also invoke Articles 25 and 26, which protect the right to freely practise religion and the right of religious denominations to manage their own affairs. Their argument is straightforward: if the state can appoint your temple's administrator, control its money, and supervise its rituals, religious freedom exists only on paper.

## Why the Court Changed Its Mind

The April 2025 order that sent petitioners to High Courts was based on a reasoning that the laws of each state "may be distinct" and therefore required separate examination. In their review petition, the petitioners dismantled this logic by showing that all four statutes share a common origin in the old Madras Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments laws and contain corresponding provisions on virtually every major point — from Commissioner powers to fee structures.

They also pointed out that the Supreme Court itself had, in earlier rounds of the same case, directed the petitions to be listed for final hearing — first in January 2016, then again in July 2016. Sending the case back to High Courts after 13 years of Supreme Court proceedings, they argued, would cause intolerable hardship and a multiplication of parallel litigation.

Senior Advocates CS Vaidyanathan and Guru Krishnakumar represented the petitioners. Solicitor General Tushar Mehta appeared for the Union of India.

## The Diaspora Connection

The question of government control over Hindu temples resonates deeply with the Indian diaspora. Many NRIs who maintain ties to ancestral temples in Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, and other southern states have watched with frustration as government-appointed administrators have been accused of mismanaging funds, neglecting infrastructure, and diverting temple revenue to non-religious purposes.

Temple donations from overseas Indians — who contribute significantly to the upkeep of major pilgrimage sites — flow into institutions where the donors have no say in governance. The contrast with self-governing religious institutions in the West, where diaspora communities often run their own temples with full financial autonomy, has fuelled a growing movement demanding that Indian temples be freed from state control.

Hindu advocacy organisations in the United States, United Kingdom, and Canada have been tracking this case for years. A ruling on the merits — whatever direction it takes — would be the most significant judicial examination of temple governance in independent India's history.

## What Comes Next

The Court has not yet scheduled the substantive hearing, but with the review petitions allowed and the 2025 order recalled, the constitutional challenge is now firmly on the Supreme Court's docket. Given the case's 13-year history, both sides will be pressing for an expedited hearing.

The political stakes are considerable. Temple administration has become a potent issue in Tamil Nadu and Andhra Pradesh politics, with multiple parties promising reforms. A Supreme Court ruling could either validate existing state control or force a fundamental restructuring of how hundreds of thousands of temples across four states are governed.

For a diaspora that has long felt its religious institutions in India are under bureaucratic siege, the revival of this case is a signal that the highest court is ready to engage with the substance — not just the procedure — of their grievance.
